ideas.cost_estimate: One additional batched quantization pass of B=8 per item; no codebook or recommender training cost change beyond the extra token vocabulary. Expected Stage2 wall time roughly 1.1–1.3x, dominated by quantization.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: On held-out next-item evaluation, adding s_i improves Recall@K/NDCG@K over the same baseline SID, with the largest gain among items whose bootstrap agreement a_i is low; verify by overall metrics and predeclared agreement-bin slices. Reject if gains are absent or confined to one unstable random seed.
ideas.key_change: Generate several perturbed views of each training item embedding, quantize each with the trained codebooks, and append a small stability token to the ordinary SID. The token summarizes agreement, allowing the generative recommender to learn when a semantic code should be interpreted coarsely versus confidently.
ideas.motivation: Items with noisy, sparse, or ambiguous content embeddings can receive brittle codes; a recommender that treats these codes as equally certain may overfit accidental distinctions and miss useful alternatives.
ideas.novelty: Rather than changing the embedding geometry or adding another interaction-transition loss, measure how stable each item's quantized code is under train-only perturbations and expose that stability in its identifier.
risks: Embedding perturbations may not reflect real metadata noise; a stability token may just encode item frequency/popularity indirectly or consume sequence-model capacity. Hard agreement can be sensitive to sigma and codebook boundaries, and appended tokens may not be consumed usefully.

specification.text: For each item i with embedding x_i, form B train-only perturbations x_i^(b)=x_i+epsilon^(b), epsilon^(b)~N(0,sigma^2 diag(v)), where v is the per-dimension variance estimated over training-item embeddings. Quantize each view with the frozen baseline quantizer to obtain tuple q_i^(b). Let a_i=(1/B) max_q sum_b 1[q_i^(b)=q]. Assign stability token s_i= min(S-1, floor(S*a_i)), with S=4 bins (use bins [0,.5), [.5,.75), [.75,.95), [.95,1]); export SID_i=(q_i,s_i). Keep perturbations and all statistics fit using training items only; apply identical deterministic seeded perturbations at export. Compare against baseline at fixed sequence model and training budget.

ideas.title: Encode semantic-boundary uncertainty as an explicit SID token

ideas.cost_estimate: Negligible: one pass over training interactions and a 12-token suffix vocabulary; no additional embedding model or quantizer training. Sequence-model cost is effectively unchanged.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: The suffix improves held-out next-item ranking over baseline, especially for repeat-consuming users and within frequency-matched item groups; measure overall Recall@K/NDCG@K and those predeclared slices. It is not worth keeping if frequency-matched performance does not improve, indicating the suffix only duplicates popularity.
ideas.key_change: Append a discretized demand-shape suffix computed from training interactions, separating repeat/revisit propensity from raw item frequency so the generative model can condition on distinct usage regimes without changing item embeddings.
ideas.motivation: Content-near items can have very different roles in user activity: some are repeatedly revisited while others are typically one-off discoveries. A content-only SID can therefore fail to distinguish items whose consumption patterns call for different continuation predictions.
ideas.novelty: This adds a low-cardinality behavioral descriptor derived from the shape of training-only item usage, not a transition/adjacency objective, graph embedding, or popularity-weighted codebook loss; the existing content SID remains unchanged.
risks: Repeat propensity is noisy for infrequent items, and per-frequency-bin quantiles may be unstable; user/item leakage can arise if boundaries accidentally use validation or test interactions. The appended behavior may be nonstationary or redundant with sequence context and could worsen cold-item generalization.

specification.text: Using training sequences only, for each item i compute f_i=count of occurrences, u_i=count of distinct training users, and r_i=(number of users with >=2 occurrences of i)/(u_i+1). Compute p_i=log(1+f_i/u_i) (set to 0 if u_i=0). Within each training-only frequency decile, quantile-bin r_i into 3 bins; independently quantile-bin p_i into 2 bins. Append suffix d_i=6*b_r+b_p to the baseline SID. Fit decile boundaries and quantiles on training items/interactions only; freeze them for validation/test. Evaluate against the unmodified baseline using the same sequence split and model settings.

ideas.title: Add a compact train-only demand-shape suffix

ideas.cost_estimate: One training-sequence pass plus sparse graph aggregation O(E*d); memory O(E). Typically <5% additional Stage2 wall time, excluding unchanged tokenizer fitting.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: At least one lambda improves held-out next-item Recall@K/NDCG@K for a recommender trained on the resulting SIDs over baseline SIDs, while increasing train-only graph-neighbor embedding similarity of same-user transitions; otherwise reject.
ideas.key_change: Build a symmetrized, popularity-corrected item transition graph from training sequences and mix each item embedding with a normalized average of its graph neighbors before the ordinary RQ-VAE fit/export.
ideas.motivation: Text or pretrained item embeddings can place substitutes far apart and near-duplicates together despite repeated user transitions; SIDs then fail to share useful prefixes for next-item generation.
ideas.novelty: Rather than feeding interaction samples into a quantizer or changing its geometry, this first constructs a bounded, item-level denoised embedding using only training sequences, then applies the existing SID tokenizer unchanged.
risks: Popular hubs can cause oversmoothing; transition edges may encode navigational rather than semantic relations; sparse/short histories yield noisy estimates. Popularity correction and small lambda may not fully prevent these effects.

specification.text: For each adjacent pair (i,j) in each training sequence increment C[i,j]. Let w_ij=(C[i,j]+C[j,i]) / ((deg_out(i)+1)^a (deg_out(j)+1)^a), with a=0.5; set P_ij=w_ij/sum_k w_ik. For each item with positive row sum, g_i=sum_j P_ij x_j, otherwise g_i=x_i. L2-normalize x_i and g_i, then x'_i=normalize((1-lambda)x_i+lambda*g_i), lambda in {0.1,0.3,0.5}. Fit and export the baseline tokenizer on x'_i; use no validation/test edges or item statistics. Compare with identical baseline configuration and select lambda only by the predeclared validation protocol.

ideas.title: Denoise item semantics with train-only transition consensus

ideas.cost_estimate: Approximately 5 baseline tokenizer fits for replicas plus one final fit (about 6x Stage2 training compute); assignment alignment costs O(B*L*K^3), negligible at K=256 relative to fitting.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: Across at least three seeds, consensus training reduces item assignment disagreement between independently fitted tokenizer seeds and improves validation next-item ranking versus the baseline at the same final-fit budget; if disagreement falls but validation ranking does not improve, discard.
ideas.key_change: Fit several lightweight tokenizer replicas on bootstrap resamples of training items, align replica code labels to a reference per codebook with Hungarian matching, then use cross-replica assignment frequencies as soft targets for a final standard tokenizer fit.
ideas.motivation: A small shift in initialization or sampled training items can move borderline products across code boundaries, making their semantic tokens unstable and depriving the generative recommender of repeatable prefix structure.
ideas.novelty: This targets tokenizer estimation uncertainty rather than adding another semantic modality, geometry, or sequential objective: train-only resampled tokenizer replicas estimate which item/code assignments are reliable, and only unstable assignments are regularized toward consensus.
risks: Code labels may not align cleanly where clusters split/merge; consensus can freeze a shared but poor local solution and reduce code utilization. Extra compute is substantial, and replica-derived targets can over-regularize rare items.

specification.text: Train B=5 replicas with the baseline architecture and hyperparameters, each sampling N training items with replacement and independent seed. For each level l, align replica code labels to replica 0 by maximum overlap of item assignments (Hungarian algorithm on the KxK overlap matrix). Define q_i,l,k=(1/B)sum_b 1[aligned_code_b(i,l)=k]. In the final tokenizer fit, retain the usual reconstruction/RQ loss and add L_cons=(gamma/(N*L))*sum_{i,l} KL(q_i,l || p_l(.|x_i)), where p is softmax of negative squared distances divided by fixed temperature tau=0.1 and gamma is selected from {0.01,0.1}; export the final model's ordinary hard assignments. All replicas and final fitting use training items only.

ideas.title: Assign IDs by bootstrap-consensus quantization

ideas.cost_estimate: About M-fold encoder computation during tokenizer training (M=2 is a minimal test); code-agreement cost is O(B*M^2*L) scalar comparisons per batch. Inference/export cost is unchanged apart from optional averaging of M embeddings.
ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: On items with high view variance v_i, the proposed tokenizer will reduce disagreement between SIDs under repeated metadata dropout by at least 25% versus baseline, while improving or preserving validation next-item Recall@10 for users whose training histories contain such items. Measure SID agreement and Recall@10 by item uncertainty quartile; reject if stability improves without a corresponding held-out recommendation benefit.
ideas.key_change: Estimate embedding uncertainty from training-only stochastic views of each item's metadata text, then train the existing RQ-VAE to reconstruct the view mean while penalizing code disagreement across views. No changes to the downstream generator or inference-time SID format are needed.
ideas.motivation: Items with sparse, ambiguous, or noisy metadata can receive brittle semantic IDs; small changes in their input embedding may send them to unrelated code paths, making generated recommendations inconsistent for the long tail.
ideas.novelty: The repository explores different quantization geometries, transition-aware residuals, and topology preservation, but does not appear to model per-item uncertainty or explicitly optimize the stability of an item's emitted code under plausible embedding perturbations.
risks: Dropout views may not reflect real metadata errors; overly large lambda can erase meaningful distinctions between near-neighbor items; short or missing metadata may produce noisy uncertainty estimates; repeated views increase training cost.

specification.text: For each training item i, encode M independently dropout-corrupted versions of its available metadata: z_i^(m)=f(x_i^(m)); let mu_i=mean_m z_i^(m), and v_i=mean_m ||z_i^(m)-mu_i||_2^2. Quantize each view to code tuple c_i^(m)=Q(z_i^(m)). Optimize L=L_RQ(mu_i,x_i)+lambda * v_i * mean_{m<n} sum_{l=1}^L 1[c_{i,l}^(m) != c_{i,l}^(n)], where L_RQ is the baseline reconstruction plus commitment objective. Use only metadata and item records in the training split; select lambda on validation. At export, assign c_i=Q(mean_m z_i^(m)).

ideas.title: Quantize stable semantics, not embedding noise

assumptions: The baseline training parquet has columns named user_id and target; the baseline already uses target as the item identifier.
Training items with no training interactions receive suffix token 0 because their r and p are both defined as zero by the specification and no within-decile training quantile can be fitted for them.

Quantile bins are assigned by stable rank within each training frequency decile, with ties resolved by input item order. This avoids ambiguous duplicate quantile edges while retaining the specified 3-bin and 2-bin quantile assignments.

The baseline collision-extension columns are retained and the demand token is appended as the final SID column, with values 0 through 11; the baseline codebook and model configuration remain unchanged.

findings.correction: Construct/count each underlying training sequence once (using stable user/order information in the frozen train data), or confirm and enforce a data contract that each row is an independent complete sequence; avoid inferring complete sequences from overlapping prefixes.
findings.detail: The graph counts every parquet training row as a complete history-plus-target sequence. If train.parquet stores the usual overlapping prefix/target examples for a user, the same underlying adjacent transition is counted repeatedly, with multiplicity dependent on how many prefixes contain it. This is not the specified one count per adjacent pair in each training sequence, and can materially skew the graph weights. The comment asserts this interpretation but does not establish that parquet rows are unique complete sequences.
findings.reproduction: Minimal counterexample: one user's sequence [a,b,c] represented by rows ([a],b) and ([a,b],c) contributes a→b twice and b→c once; a single complete-sequence pass contributes each edge once. Run denoise_with_train_transitions on those rows and compare its counts with the specified sequence counts.

findings.correction: Run the three specified lambda candidates under identical frozen inputs/configuration and select only using the predeclared validation protocol, or explicitly scope this artifact as the 0.1 candidate and defer selection to an existing downstream protocol.
findings.detail: The implementation hard-codes lambda=0.1 and labels it a fixed candidate; it does not implement the specified candidate set {0.1, 0.3, 0.5} or the predeclared validation-based selection protocol. This is a mismatch in the requested mechanism/experiment, although a single candidate run could be an explicitly staged first experiment.
findings.reproduction: Inspect GRAPH_LAMBDA and its sole use at lines 229-230 and 335: the trainer always uses 0.1, irrespective of validation results, and never evaluates the other two candidates.

findings.correction: Export an explicit raw-item-ID-to-SID mapping using item_ids.json (and arrange the NPY according to the downstream contract), or document and verify that all downstream consumers use embedding-row IDs. Add a validation that every source item maps to the intended exported row.
findings.detail: The export uses embedding-row indices as SID keys/array positions, but remap_train_item_ids explicitly maps raw parquet item IDs to embedding rows, and EMBEDDING_IDS_FILE provides the inverse mapping. The export therefore loses the raw item-ID mapping. It is only correctly indexed if every downstream consumer independently treats the embedding row as the item ID; that is not validated here, and the JSON keys are explicitly row enumerations rather than the source item IDs. This can assign SIDs to the wrong items or make non-contiguous IDs inaccessible.
findings.reproduction: Use item_ids.json=[20,10] and two embedding rows. remap_train_item_ids maps raw item 20→row 0 and 10→row 1, but export writes JSON keys "0" and "1" and sid array positions 0 and 1. A consumer looking up raw item 20 cannot retrieve its SID by that ID.

findings.correction: Recover one ordered training sequence per user from the frozen train rows (for example, deduplicate by user and reconstruct the observed train prefix through its largest target position), then count each adjacent pair exactly once; alternatively deduplicate the repeated prefix transitions with a rigorously defined per-user edge set/count before applying the stated formula.
findings.detail: The Stage0 train parquet stores one row per training prefix/target, not one row per complete training sequence. Concatenating each row's history and target therefore counts earlier transitions repeatedly. For a sequence [a,b,c], its rows contribute a→b once from target b and a→b plus b→c from target c, so the graph is not the specified once-per-adjacent-pair training-sequence graph. This changes both transition counts and popularity correction and can materially overweight early transitions.
findings.reproduction: Use the Stage0 prefix construction at stage0_build_parquet/build_recbole_parquet.py:164-170 with a single user's sequence [a,b,c]. Feeding those rows to denoise_with_train_transitions yields C[a,b]=2 and C[b,c]=1, rather than 1 and 1.

per_scorer_rationale.scoring_1: The idea makes per-item quantization robustness observable to the generator through an explicit low-cardinality SID token, a relatively uncommon intervention compared with modifying quantizer geometry. The motivation is sound for borderline or noisy embeddings, and the specification is straightforward to implement with frozen codebooks and fixed-model evaluation. Potential benefits are targeted to uncertain items rather than necessarily broad ranking gains.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: Explicitly exposing item-level quantization stability as a compact SID feature is a plausible, lightweight way to let the generator distinguish reliable from borderline codes. The idea is motivated by brittleness and is straightforward to test without changing the tokenizer or recommender objective.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: A practical way to expose quantization-boundary confidence to a generator without refitting the tokenizer. The uncertainty signal is well motivated for brittle assignments, and the single-pass perturb-and-quantize procedure is implementable at low cost. Its impact depends on whether embedding perturbations represent meaningful uncertainty and whether the generator can use the appended token rather than treating it as a nuisance feature.

per_scorer_rationale.scoring_1: Separating repeat propensity and per-user occurrence intensity from raw frequency addresses a plausible mismatch between content similarity and behavioral role. It is highly implementable using training interactions alone and yields a clear test of whether behavioral regimes add information beyond popularity. The compact suffix could affect multiple ranking slices, though it may be redundant with sequence context.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: A compact, train-only descriptor of repeat propensity and per-user demand shape addresses a real limitation of content-only identifiers: content similarity need not imply similar consumption behavior. It is cheap to implement and preserves the existing content SID, while the frequency-matched evaluation gives a meaningful test of information beyond raw popularity.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: Separating revisit propensity from raw frequency addresses a real limitation of content-only identifiers and yields a simple, interpretable behavioral suffix. It is inexpensive, uses training interactions, and offers direct tests within frequency-matched groups. It is distinct from semantic quantizer changes because it adds a train-only demand descriptor while leaving the content SID intact.

per_scorer_rationale.scoring_1: The proposal uses training-only transition consensus to adjust item representations before applying an otherwise unchanged tokenizer. This is a plausible way to reconcile content semantics with observed sequential substitutability, with a bounded mixing coefficient and a clear ablation. Sparse graph aggregation is practical at typical recommender scales, and improved representations could benefit the downstream generator broadly.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: Using train-only transitions to make a bounded, popularity-corrected adjustment to item representations is a coherent way to reconcile content semantics with observed sequential substitutability before applying an unchanged tokenizer. Sparse graph aggregation and a small lambda sweep are practical, and the mechanism is distinct from transition-loss or graph-embedding approaches.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: The proposal uses observed training transitions to make content representations more behaviorally coherent before applying an otherwise unchanged tokenizer. This is a plausible response to semantic-neighbor failures, with a bounded mixing coefficient and a straightforward held-out recommendation test. Sparse aggregation is practical for typical item-transition graphs, and the intervention is experimentally separable from adding behavioral tokens or auxiliary losses.

per_scorer_rationale.scoring_1: This directly targets tokenizer estimation uncertainty across resampled training sets and uses aligned assignment frequencies as a training signal, which is experimentally distinct from per-item perturbation tokens or behavioral augmentation. The method is implementable with standard clustering alignment and a specified consistency loss, but entails substantial repeated tokenizer training. More stable assignments are valuable only if the resulting code structure also helps recommendation.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: The proposal directly addresses tokenizer estimation variability through resampled replicas and aligned assignment consensus, which is conceptually distinct from input-uncertainty modeling or adding behavioral features. Soft consensus targets provide an implementable regularization mechanism and testable stability objective.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: This directly targets tokenizer estimation variance rather than uncertainty in the embedding or interaction features, and proposes a specific consensus-regularized final fit. It is scientifically motivated by unstable code assignments and is clearly distinct from the other interventions. If it improves both assignment reproducibility and recommendation, it could make learned SIDs more robust across runs and samples.

per_scorer_rationale.scoring_1: The idea brings stochastic metadata-view uncertainty into tokenizer training and seeks stable codes without changing the inference-time SID format, directly addressing robustness in the representation rather than exposing uncertainty as another token. It has a measurable stability target and a downstream ranking test. The approach is implementable, although encoder-view generation and the coupled agreement objective add training complexity.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: Training the tokenizer with multiple stochastic metadata views and an explicit code-agreement penalty targets stability at representation-learning time while keeping inference-time SID format unchanged. This is a principled extension of uncertainty-aware quantization, with a specific high-uncertainty subgroup hypothesis and recommendation-level evaluation.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: The proposal integrates stochastic-view uncertainty into tokenizer training and aims to produce stable ordinary SIDs, avoiding downstream vocabulary or inference-format changes. It is a meaningful extension beyond measuring stability after quantization because it explicitly regularizes assignments during fitting and weights disagreement by view variance. The connection between stable codes and long-tail recommendation consistency is plausible and testable.

scores.rationale: The idea makes per-item quantization robustness observable to the generator through an explicit low-cardinality SID token, a relatively uncommon intervention compared with modifying quantizer geometry. The motivation is sound for borderline or noisy embeddings, and the specification is straightforward to implement with frozen codebooks and fixed-model evaluation. Potential benefits are targeted to uncertain items rather than necessarily broad ranking gains.
scores.uncertainties: Gaussian perturbations based on embedding variance may not correspond to realistic metadata or representation uncertainty. Results may depend strongly on sigma and binning, and the token could act as a nuisance or correlate with item popularity rather than provide useful confidence information.

scores.rationale: Separating repeat propensity and per-user occurrence intensity from raw frequency addresses a plausible mismatch between content similarity and behavioral role. It is highly implementable using training interactions alone and yields a clear test of whether behavioral regimes add information beyond popularity. The compact suffix could affect multiple ranking slices, though it may be redundant with sequence context.
scores.uncertainties: Repeat estimates for rare items can be noisy, and the proposed within-decile quantiles may be unstable in small datasets. It is uncertain whether the suffix encodes behavior beyond frequency or user-history context, and whether training-derived demand regimes generalize over time or to cold items.

scores.rationale: The proposal uses training-only transition consensus to adjust item representations before applying an otherwise unchanged tokenizer. This is a plausible way to reconcile content semantics with observed sequential substitutability, with a bounded mixing coefficient and a clear ablation. Sparse graph aggregation is practical at typical recommender scales, and improved representations could benefit the downstream generator broadly.
scores.uncertainties: Transition proximity may reflect navigation or co-consumption rather than semantic substitutability; popular nodes and sparse histories may distort the aggregate. The outcome may depend on graph construction, normalization, lambda, and whether the transition graph adds information beyond the sequence model itself.

scores.rationale: This directly targets tokenizer estimation uncertainty across resampled training sets and uses aligned assignment frequencies as a training signal, which is experimentally distinct from per-item perturbation tokens or behavioral augmentation. The method is implementable with standard clustering alignment and a specified consistency loss, but entails substantial repeated tokenizer training. More stable assignments are valuable only if the resulting code structure also helps recommendation.
scores.uncertainties: Hungarian matching may not resolve split/merge differences across replicas, particularly at deeper codebook levels. The consensus targets may preserve an arbitrary shared solution, harm code utilization, or over-regularize rare items; the sizeable compute cost makes adequate seed replication and tuning harder.

scores.rationale: The idea brings stochastic metadata-view uncertainty into tokenizer training and seeks stable codes without changing the inference-time SID format, directly addressing robustness in the representation rather than exposing uncertainty as another token. It has a measurable stability target and a downstream ranking test. The approach is implementable, although encoder-view generation and the coupled agreement objective add training complexity.
scores.uncertainties: Metadata dropout may be a poor proxy for actual ambiguity or input corruption, and the variance-weighted disagreement term could suppress meaningful distinctions. The formula's interaction between uncertainty magnitude, pairwise code disagreement, and reconstruction objective may require careful scaling; recommendation gains on high-uncertainty histories are not assured.

scores.rationale: Explicitly exposing item-level quantization stability as a compact SID feature is a plausible, lightweight way to let the generator distinguish reliable from borderline codes. The idea is motivated by brittleness and is straightforward to test without changing the tokenizer or recommender objective.
scores.uncertainties: Gaussian perturbations based on embedding-coordinate variance may not represent realistic metadata uncertainty; stability may mostly reflect codebook geometry, and the generator may ignore or misuse the extra token. Magnitude and robustness of ranking gains are unknown.

scores.rationale: A compact, train-only descriptor of repeat propensity and per-user demand shape addresses a real limitation of content-only identifiers: content similarity need not imply similar consumption behavior. It is cheap to implement and preserves the existing content SID, while the frequency-matched evaluation gives a meaningful test of information beyond raw popularity.
scores.uncertainties: Repeat statistics can be noisy for sparse items and may encode popularity or dataset-specific behavior rather than transferable demand regimes. It is unclear how much information remains after conditioning on frequency and sequence context, and whether the signature generalizes to cold items or shifting demand.

scores.rationale: Using train-only transitions to make a bounded, popularity-corrected adjustment to item representations is a coherent way to reconcile content semantics with observed sequential substitutability before applying an unchanged tokenizer. Sparse graph aggregation and a small lambda sweep are practical, and the mechanism is distinct from transition-loss or graph-embedding approaches.
scores.uncertainties: Transition neighbors may capture navigation or co-occurrence rather than semantic substitutes, and hubs or sparse histories can distort the aggregate despite correction. The proposed similarity check does not establish improved semantic quality; effects on recommendation quality and long-tail items remain empirical.

scores.rationale: The proposal directly addresses tokenizer estimation variability through resampled replicas and aligned assignment consensus, which is conceptually distinct from input-uncertainty modeling or adding behavioral features. Soft consensus targets provide an implementable regularization mechanism and testable stability objective.
scores.uncertainties: Replica labels may not admit reliable one-to-one alignment when codebooks split or merge, particularly across residual quantization levels. Six tokenizer fits are a substantial cost, and lower assignment disagreement may not improve recommendation ranking or could reduce code utilization.

scores.rationale: Training the tokenizer with multiple stochastic metadata views and an explicit code-agreement penalty targets stability at representation-learning time while keeping inference-time SID format unchanged. This is a principled extension of uncertainty-aware quantization, with a specific high-uncertainty subgroup hypothesis and recommendation-level evaluation.
scores.uncertainties: Metadata dropout may not approximate actual ambiguity or corruption, and the variance-weighted penalty could either over-regularize meaningful distinctions or underweight noisy views depending on scale. Multi-view encoder computation adds cost; whether improved code stability translates to held-out recommendation gains is unknown.

scores.rationale: A practical way to expose quantization-boundary confidence to a generator without refitting the tokenizer. The uncertainty signal is well motivated for brittle assignments, and the single-pass perturb-and-quantize procedure is implementable at low cost. Its impact depends on whether embedding perturbations represent meaningful uncertainty and whether the generator can use the appended token rather than treating it as a nuisance feature.
scores.uncertainties: The variance-scaled Gaussian perturbation and sigma are not calibrated to metadata corruption; agreement may mostly report distance to code boundaries rather than epistemic or semantic uncertainty. The binning specification has overlapping endpoint ambiguity at a_i=0.5, 0.75, and 0.95, and deterministic perturbations need careful reproducibility. No evidence yet that this feature improves recommendation rather than simply encoding item-specific tokenizer geometry.

scores.rationale: Separating revisit propensity from raw frequency addresses a real limitation of content-only identifiers and yields a simple, interpretable behavioral suffix. It is inexpensive, uses training interactions, and offers direct tests within frequency-matched groups. It is distinct from semantic quantizer changes because it adds a train-only demand descriptor while leaving the content SID intact.
scores.uncertainties: Repeat propensity may be poorly estimated for rare items, and the per-decile quantile bins may be degenerate or unstable when deciles have few distinct items. The signal could be redundant with sequence context or act as a popularity proxy; stationarity and cold-item behavior are unestablished. Clarify handling of empty/undersized bins and unseen items.

scores.rationale: The proposal uses observed training transitions to make content representations more behaviorally coherent before applying an otherwise unchanged tokenizer. This is a plausible response to semantic-neighbor failures, with a bounded mixing coefficient and a straightforward held-out recommendation test. Sparse aggregation is practical for typical item-transition graphs, and the intervention is experimentally separable from adding behavioral tokens or auxiliary losses.
scores.uncertainties: Transition adjacency can reflect navigation, position, or popularity rather than substitutability, so graph smoothing may blur useful distinctions. The degree correction uses out-degrees even though the edge weight is symmetrized; the intended degree definition and treatment of self-edges/zero rows should be explicit. Benefits may depend strongly on graph sparsity, lambda, and sequence construction.

scores.rationale: This directly targets tokenizer estimation variance rather than uncertainty in the embedding or interaction features, and proposes a specific consensus-regularized final fit. It is scientifically motivated by unstable code assignments and is clearly distinct from the other interventions. If it improves both assignment reproducibility and recommendation, it could make learned SIDs more robust across runs and samples.
scores.uncertainties: The method is implementable but requires roughly six tokenizer fits, making compute and iteration cost substantial. Hungarian alignment may conceal split/merge structure and force misleading one-to-one correspondences; q targets may be diffuse or inconsistent. The KL direction, handling of codebook-level alignment across residual levels, temperature calibration, and whether replica targets are computed for every item need validation. Reduced assignment disagreement may not translate into ranking gains.

scores.rationale: The proposal integrates stochastic-view uncertainty into tokenizer training and aims to produce stable ordinary SIDs, avoiding downstream vocabulary or inference-format changes. It is a meaningful extension beyond measuring stability after quantization because it explicitly regularizes assignments during fitting and weights disagreement by view variance. The connection between stable codes and long-tail recommendation consistency is plausible and testable.
scores.uncertainties: Feasibility depends on access to the metadata encoder and a well-defined dropout/corruption mechanism; M-view encoding raises training cost and the loss can be sensitive to lambda and view generation. As written, the variance multiplier may give high-uncertainty items more disagreement penalty, but its scale relative to the baseline loss is unspecified. The notation L_RQ(mu_i,x_i) needs clarification if x_i is text or an embedding target. Dropout variance may not reflect real metadata noise, and improved SID stability may not improve recommendation quality.
